proofs.proof_tex:
Write
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}
 =\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}^{\partial}
   (d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa).
\]
The hypotheses that \(m\) is odd, every arrow \(j\to i\) in \(G\) satisfies
\(j<i\), and \(u\to v\in G\) are precisely the parity, order, and queried-edge
conditions used below.  By
\(\mathrm{lem{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}class\mbox{-}nonempty}\),
the additional displayed hypothesis
\[
 \kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}                                      \tag{1}
\]
implies \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\ne\varnothing\).  Thus the uniform
assertion is not vacuous.  In what follows \(d,m,G,\mathcal Z,\gamma,L,
d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa\) are fixed, \(\mathcal Z\) is finite and
nonempty, \(n\to\infty\), and every supremum is over
\(P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\).

First we record the uniform conditioning needed for the recursive map.  After
identifying each stationary law with its fine parameter \((A,D)\), the
parameter set underlying \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\) is compact.  Indeed,
\(\mathrm{def{:}regular\mbox{-}class}\) and
\(\mathrm{def{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}class}\)
impose the closed graph-zero restrictions and the closed inequalities
\[
 |A_{ij}|\le L,\qquad |A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma,
 \qquad d_{\min}I_d\preceq D\preceq d_{\max}I_d,              \tag{2}
\]
\[
 \min_{j\to i\in G}|C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\ge\kappa,
 \qquad
 \min_{i\in V}m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\ge\kappa.                      \tag{3}
\]
The bounds in \((2)\) make this closed set bounded.  Its lower innovation
bound makes \(D\) positive definite.  Because \(A\) is lower triangular,
its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, so \((2)\) gives
\(\rho(A)\le1-\gamma<1\).  The Gaussian-innovation condition in
\(\mathrm{def{:}regular\mbox{-}class}\) therefore associates a unique
stationary Gaussian law with every admissible \((A,D)\).

Put
\[
 \vartheta=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(M_0,M_1),\qquad
 \widehat\vartheta=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(\widehat M_0,\widehat M_1),
 \qquad \rho=1-\gamma.
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}coarse\mbox{-}law\mbox{-}reduction}\),
\[
 Y_s=BY_{s-1}+\eta_s,\qquad B=A^m,
 \qquad
 \eta_s\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}
 \sigma(Y_{s-1},Y_{s-2},\ldots),
 \qquad \eta_s\sim N(0,Q),                                  \tag{4}
\]
and
\[
 B=M_1M_0^{-1},qquad Q=M_0-BM_0B^\top.                       \tag{5}
\]
The innovation lower bound and the definition of \(Q\) yield
\[
 Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top\succeq D
   \succeq d_{\min}I_d.                                      \tag{6}
\]
Iteration of the stable recursion in \((4)\), or equivalently grouping the
fine-grid stationary covariance series into blocks of length \(m\), gives
\[
 M_0=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^kQ(B^k)^\top
     =\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}A^rD(A^r)^\top
     \succeq Q\succeq d_{\min}I_d.                            \tag{7}
\]
There is also a uniform upper bound.  In an entry of \(A^r\), lower
triangularity permits only nondecreasing vertex walks.  Such a walk has at
most \(d-1\) strict increases; choosing their locations contributes at most
a polynomial of degree \(d-1\), every strict-increase factor is bounded by
\(L\), and every remaining factor is diagonal and bounded by \(\rho\).
Consequently there is a finite constant \(C_A=C_A(d,L,\rho)\) such that
\[
 \lVert A^r\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le C_A(r+1)^{d-1}\rho^{(r-d+1)_+},\qquad r\ge0.             \tag{8}
\]
The upper innovation bound and \((8)\) imply
\[
 M_0\preceq
 d_{\max}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\lVert A^r\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2I_d
 \preceq C_0I_d                                             \tag{9}
\]
for a finite \(C_0=C_0(d,L,\gamma,d_{\max})\).  Equations
\((7)\)--\((9)\) make inversion of \(M_0\) uniformly legitimate.  Hence
the moment-to-coarse-parameter map
\[
 (M_0,M_1)\longmapsto(B,Q)
 =\bigl(M_1M_0^{-1},\ M_0-M_1M_0^{-1}M_1^\top\bigr)          \tag{10}
\]
is twice continuously differentiable, with uniformly bounded first and
second derivatives on one open neighborhood of the compact population
moment set.

We next treat the graph-recursive inverse.  Since \(B_{ii}=A_{ii}^m\), the
second inequality in \((3)\) gives
\[
 \left|\frac{\partial B_{ii}}{\partial A_{ii}}\right|
 =m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\ge\kappa.                                 \tag{11}
\]
Oddness of \(m\) makes the real diagonal root unique.  Its first derivative
with respect to \(B_{ii}\) is \((mA_{ii}^{m-1})^{-1}\), and its second
derivative is
\[
 -\frac{m-1}{m^2A_{ii}^{2m-1}}.
\]
Both are uniformly bounded, because \((11)\) implies
\(|A_{ii}|\ge(\kappa/m)^{1/(m-1)}>0\).  For an allowed off-diagonal
coordinate, the first inequality in \((3)\) and
\(\mathrm{thm{:}odd\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}identification}\) give the
recursion
\[
 A_{ij}
 =\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})},
 \qquad |C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\ge\kappa.                       \tag{12}
\]
At endpoint gap \(i-j\), every coordinate occurring in the polynomial
\(R_{ij,m}\) has already been recovered at a smaller endpoint gap.  Starting
with the diagonal roots and inducting over the finitely many gaps, \((12)\)
therefore expresses every recovered coordinate as a twice continuously
differentiable function of \(B\).  Compactness and continuity provide a
common neighborhood on which every denominator in \((11)\)--\((12)\) has
absolute value at least \(\kappa/2\); on that neighborhood all first and
second derivatives of the full recursion are uniformly bounded.  The
innovation recursion in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}odd\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}identification}\) is smooth as
well, since each of its denominators obeys
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}\ge1.                            \tag{13}
\]

For \(z\in\mathcal Z\subset\mathbb T\), the stability margin gives
\[
 |1-A_{vv}z|\ge1-|A_{vv}|\ge\gamma.                         \tag{14}
\]
Thus the coefficient-to-transfer map is twice continuously differentiable
on the same common neighborhood.  Direct differentiation of
\(h_{uv}(z)=A_{vu}z/(1-A_{vv}z)\) gives
\[
 \mathrm dh_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{z\,\mathrm dA_{vu}}{1-A_{vv}z}
  +\frac{A_{vu}z^2\,\mathrm dA_{vv}}{(1-A_{vv}z)^2}.         \tag{15}
\]
Let \(F(\vartheta)\) stack the real and imaginary parts of
\((h_{uv}(z))_{z\in\mathcal Z}\), and let \(J_h(\vartheta)\) be the
Jacobian of the composite of \((10)\), the graph recursion, and \((15)\).
The uniform second-derivative bound just proved gives the Taylor expansion
\[
 F(\widehat\vartheta)-F(\vartheta)
 =J_h(\vartheta)(\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)+r_n,
 \qquad
 \lVert r_n\rVert\le C\lVert\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta\rVert^2           \tag{16}
\]
whenever \(\widehat\vartheta\) lies in the common neighborhood.  By
\(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\mbox{-}gaussian\mbox{-}lag\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}clt}\),
\(\sqrt n(\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)\) is uniformly tight and converges
uniformly to \(N(0,\Omega(P))\), where
\[
 \Omega(P)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}_P(g_0,g_k).             \tag{17}
\]
Uniform tightness makes the neighborhood event in \((16)\) have probability
tending to one uniformly and, for each \(\epsilon>0\), yields
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 P\!\left(\sqrt n\lVert r_n\rVert>\epsilon\right)
 \longrightarrow0.                                          \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, on an event where
\(\sqrt n\lVert\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta\rVert\le K\), the right-hand
side of \((16)\), after multiplication by \(\sqrt n\), is at most
\(CK^2/\sqrt n\), while the complementary probability can be made uniformly
small by choosing \(K\) large.  Equations \((16)\)--\((18)\) establish the
uniform limit
\[
 \sqrt n\{F(\widehat\vartheta)-F(\vartheta)\}
 \Longrightarrow N(0,\Sigma_h(P)),
 \qquad
 \Sigma_h(P)=J_h(\vartheta)\Omega(P)J_h(\vartheta)^\top.     \tag{19}
\]
This is exactly the Gaussian law obtained by applying the stated recursive
Jacobian and the differential \((15)\) to the long-run lag-moment covariance.

We now verify uniform covariance estimation.  The covariance series in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\mbox{-}gaussian\mbox{-}lag\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}clt}\)
converges absolutely and uniformly, and each Gaussian Isserlis summand is a
continuous polynomial in the coarse covariance sequence.  It follows that
\(P\mapsto\Omega(P)\), and hence \(P\mapsto\Sigma_h(P)\), is continuous on
the compact parameter set.  Let \(\widetilde\Omega\) be the Isserlis plug-in
estimator furnished by that lemma, and let \(\widehat\Omega\) be its
positive-semidefinite projection.  Since the eigenvalues of
\(B=A^m\) have modulus at most \((1-\gamma)^m<1\), compactness and continuity
of spectral radius give a common neighborhood of the population \(B\)'s
consisting of stable matrices.  Uniform consistency of \(\widehat B\), which
follows from \((10)\) and the uniform tightness above, therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 P(\widehat B\text{ is not stable})\longrightarrow0.         \tag{20}
\]
On the event in \((20)\)'s complement, the cited lag-moment lemma gives
\(\widetilde\Omega-\Omega(P)=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly.  Since
\(\Omega(P)\) itself is positive semidefinite, the defining least-distance
property of the projection and the triangle inequality give
\[
 \lVert\widehat\Omega-\Omega(P)\rVert_F
 \le2\lVert\widetilde\Omega-\Omega(P)\rVert_F,
\]
so \(\widehat\Omega-\Omega(P)=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly.  The smoothness
already proved also gives
\(\widehat J_h-J_h=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly.  Consequently
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_h
 =\widehat J_h\widehat\Omega\widehat J_h^\top
 =\Sigma_h(P)+o_{\mathbb P}(1)                               \tag{21}
\]
uniformly, and \(\widehat\Sigma_h\) is positive semidefinite.

It remains to justify the Gaussian critical value uniformly even when the
cross-frequency covariance changes rank.  Define the regressor moment
\[
 \widetilde M_0=n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}Y_{s-1}Y_{s-1}^\top.
\]
The empirical-moment definition gives the exact boundary identity
\[
 \widehat M_0-\widetilde M_0
 =n^{-1}(Y_nY_n^\top-Y_0Y_0^\top).                           \tag{22}
\]
The uniform covariance bound \((9)\) implies, by the first-moment bound
applied to the Frobenius norm of the right-hand side, that \((22)\) is
\(o_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\) uniformly.  From \((4)\),
\[
 \widehat M_1
 =B\widetilde M_0+n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\eta_sY_{s-1}^\top.
\]
Using \((7)\), \((22)\), and the first-order inverse expansion in the
uniformly conditioned neighborhood gives
\[
 \sqrt n\,\operatorname{vec}(\widehat B-B)
 =\operatorname{vec}\!\left(
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\eta_sY_{s-1}^\top M_0^{-1}
 \right)+o_{\mathbb P}(1)                                   \tag{23}
\]
uniformly.  The summands are martingale differences by the independence in
\((4)\).  Their covariance, up to the fixed vectorization convention, is
\[
 \Gamma_B=M_0^{-1}\otimes Q.
\]
Equations \((6)\), \((7)\), and \((9)\) imply
\[
 \Gamma_B\succeq c_BI_{d^2},
 \qquad c_B=\frac{d_{\min}}{C_0}>0.                          \tag{24}
\]

Because \(u\to v\in G\), the recursion \((12)\) recovers \(A_{vu}\) as
an allowed coordinate, and its remainder uses only smaller endpoint gaps.
The diagonal roots do not depend on \(B_{vu}\).  Hence
\[
 \frac{\partial A_{vu}}{\partial B_{vu}}
 =\frac{1}{C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})},
 \qquad
 \frac{\partial A_{vv}}{\partial B_{vu}}=0.                 \tag{25}
\]
Since \(|A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma<1\) and \(|z|=1\),
\[
 |C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})|
 \le\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}|A_{vv}|^r|A_{uu}|^{m-1-r}\le m,
 \qquad |1-A_{vv}z|\le2.                                   \tag{26}
\]
Combining \((15)\), \((25)\), and \((26)\) gives
\[
 \left|\frac{\partial h_{uv}(z)}{\partial B_{vu}}\right|
 =\frac{1}{|C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})|\,|1-A_{vv}z|}
 \ge\frac1{2m}.                                             \tag{27}
\]
Thus \((23)\)--\((27)\) imply, for every \(z\in\mathcal Z\), that the
limiting complex coordinate \(Z_h(z)\) in \((19)\) satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E_P|Z_h(z)|^2\ge\frac{c_B}{4m^2}>0                 \tag{28}
\]
uniformly.  In particular, the limiting real covariance vector is never the
zero matrix, although it may be singular because coordinates at distinct
frequencies can be linearly dependent.  Notice that this argument does not
require \(A_{vu}\ne0\).

For a real vector arranged in complex-coordinate pairs, set
\[
 \lVert x\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}
 =\max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt{x_{\Re,z}^2+x_{\Im,z}^2}.
\]
The condition \(\mathrm{ass{:}confidence\mbox{-}level}\) gives
\(0<1-\alpha<1\).  For \(\Sigma\succeq0\), let
\(Z_\Sigma\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) and define
\[
 c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma)
 =\inf\{t:\Pr(\lVert Z_\Sigma\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}\le t)
 \ge1-\alpha\}.                                            \tag{29}
\]
The covariance range
\(\{\Sigma_h(P):P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\}\) is compact by continuity,
and \((28)\) keeps it away from the zero matrix.  On the support subspace of
any nonzero centered Gaussian vector, the Gaussian law has a positive
density and the restriction of \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}\)
is a norm.  A norm sphere has Lebesgue measure zero in that subspace, whereas
every nonempty norm annulus has positive measure.  Therefore the distribution
function in \((29)\) is continuous and strictly increasing on
\((0,\infty)\), and it has no atom at zero.

If \(\Sigma_j\to\Sigma\), continuity of the positive-semidefinite square
root permits the coupling
\(Z_{\Sigma_j}=\Sigma_j^{1/2}\xi\to\Sigma^{1/2}\xi=Z_\Sigma\) almost surely
for \(\xi\sim N(0,I)\).  At the two points bracketing the unique quantile in
\((29)\), the just-proved strict continuity then sandwiches the corresponding
quantiles.  Hence
\[
 c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_j)\longrightarrow c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma).              \tag{30}
\]
Compactness makes this continuity uniform on a neighborhood of the covariance
range.  Taking
\(\widehat c_{1-\alpha}=c_{1-\alpha}(\widehat\Sigma_h)\), equations
\((21)\) and \((30)\) give
\[
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}
 =c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_h(P))+o_{\mathbb P}(1)                 \tag{31}
\]
uniformly.

Finally, suppose the asserted uniform coverage failed.  Then there would be
a sequence \(P_n\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\) along which the absolute
coverage error stayed bounded away from zero.  Compactness supplies a
subsequence on which the fine parameters converge; continuity then gives
\(\Sigma_h(P_n)\to\Sigma_*\).  The uniform convergence in \((19)\) makes the
centered statistic along that subsequence converge to \(N(0,\Sigma_*)\), and
\((31)\) makes its random critical value converge in probability to
\(c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_*)\).  The boundary
\(\{x:\lVert x\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}=c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_*)\}\) has
zero probability by the argument following \((29)\).  It follows that
\[
 \Pr_{P_n}\!\left{
 \max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt n\,
 |\widehat h_{uv}(z)-h_{uv}(z)|
 \le\widehat c_{1-\alpha}
 \right}\longrightarrow1-\alpha,                           \tag{32}
\]
contradicting the chosen sequence.  The event in \((32)\) is exactly
\[
 h_{uv}(z)\in
 \left\{w\in\mathbb C:
 |w-\widehat h_{uv}(z)|\le
 \frac{\widehat c_{1-\alpha}}{\sqrt n}
 \right\}
 \quad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z.
\]
Thus its coverage converges to \(1-\alpha\) uniformly over the explicitly
nonempty derivative-separated class, completing the proof.

Formally specialize the constructions in Definition~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber} and Definition~\texttt{def:certificate} to \(m=1\).  If \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\), the first compatibility equation gives
\[
B=A^1=A.
\]
The second compatibility equation, together with \(A^0=I_d\), gives
\[
Q=\sum_{r=0}^{1-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top
  =A^0D(A^0)^\top
  =D.
\]
Thus every member of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) equals \((B,Q)\), and the fiber has at most one member.  Conversely, substituting \((A,D)=(B,Q)\) into Definition~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber} shows that \((B,Q)\) is in the fiber if and only if
\[
B_{ij}=0\quad(i<j),
\qquad
B_{ij}=0\quad(i>j\text{ and }j\to i\notin G),
\]
\[
\max_i|B_{ii}|<1,
\qquad
Q_{ij}=0\quad(i\ne j),
\qquad
Q\succ0.
\]
These are exactly the fine-grid compatibility constraints appearing in that definition after the specialization.  Hence
\[
\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=
\begin{cases}
\{(B,Q)\},&\text{if all of the displayed constraints hold},\\
\varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

It remains to check the output of the algorithm rather than infer it only from the cardinality of the fiber.  On the specialization \(m=1\), every diagonal root equation enumerated by \(\operatorname{Cert}_{uv,1,G}\) is
\[
a_{ii}^{,1}=B_{ii},
\]
so it has the unique real solution \(a_{ii}=B_{ii}\).  From the declared divided-difference polynomial,
\[
C_1(x,y)=\sum_{r=0}^{0}x^r y^{0-r}=1.
\]
A nondecreasing walk of length one has at most one strict increase.  Therefore the declared sum defining the indirect-path remainder has an empty index set and
\[
R_{vu,1}(A)=0.
\]
Consequently, at every lower-triangular coordinate processed by the recursion in Definition~\texttt{def:certificate}, the root identity reduces to
\[
B_{vu}=A_{vu}C_1(A_{vv},A_{uu})+R_{vu,1}(A)=A_{vu}.
\]
Thus every divided-difference coefficient is nonsingular, the recursive enumeration has the sole transition candidate \(A=B\), and the coarse covariance equation has the sole innovation candidate \(D=Q\).  The exact compatibility test in the certificate rejects this candidate precisely when one of the defining fiber constraints fails.  In that event the fiber is empty by the preceding equivalence, and the certificate returns incompatibility.  Otherwise it accepts \((B,Q)\).  Since both copies in the certificate's two-copy transfer-inequality test must then equal this same pair, that inequality system is infeasible, and the common-transfer branch returns
\[
h_{uv}(z)
=\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}
=\frac{B_{vu}z}{1-B_{vv}z}.
\]
Finally, accepted compatibility gives \(|B_{vv}|<1\).  For every \(z\in\mathbb T\), \(|z|=1\), and hence
\[
|B_{vv}z|=|B_{vv}|<1.
\]
It follows that \(1-B_{vv}z\ne0\), so the displayed rational function is well defined on \(\mathbb T\).  This is exactly the fine-grid direct process transfer, proving the proposition.
